# Platform Engineering — Accelerated Leadership Course

Advanced software engineering • Technical Lead / Principal Engineer / Software Architect / Engineering Manager

(2 hours 40 minutes) (8 modules) (Architecture & leadership)

## Course objective

Platform Engineering is the discipline of building **internal products, tools, infrastructure, and standardized workflows that make software delivery easier, safer, and more reliable for development teams.**

At a senior engineering level, the challenge is not simply knowing how to implement a platform. It is understanding\:

- What should be centralized versus owned by application teams.
- How to reduce developer complexity without limiting engineering flexibility.
- When standardization creates value and when it becomes bureaucracy.
- How to build platforms that teams actually want to adopt.
- How to measure whether platform investments improve organizational performance.

Given your experience with shared backend services, multi-tenancy, feature flag management, developer tooling, Azure, and Kubernetes, many of these concepts will be familiar. The goal is to connect those experiences into a coherent platform engineering strategy.

## Course roadmap

---

# Module 1 — Platform Engineering Fundamentals

20 minutes

## 1.1 Why platform engineering exists

Consider an enterprise with 40 development teams maintaining 150 applications.

Every team needs to\:

- Create and configure environments.
- Deploy applications.
- Manage secrets and configuration.
- Implement authentication and authorization.
- Configure logging and monitoring.
- Set up CI/CD pipelines.
- Apply security policies.
- Diagnose production incidents.

Without a common platform, teams repeatedly solve the same problems.

One team creates deployment scripts using GitHub Actions. Another uses Jenkins. A third maintains custom PowerShell scripts.

Each team independently configures monitoring, secrets, networking, and infrastructure.

The result is **duplicated engineering effort, inconsistent security, unpredictable deployments, and increased operational complexity**\.

Platform engineering addresses this by turning common engineering capabilities into reusable, supported services.

Without a platform

---

With a platform

Application teams retain ownership of their software while consuming standardized platform capabilities.

The important shift is that infrastructure and delivery capabilities become **products consumed by developers**, rather than isolated operational tasks.

## 1.2 Platform Engineering versus DevOps versus SRE

These disciplines overlap, but their primary responsibilities differ.

| Discipline | Primary focus |
|--------|--------|
| DevOps | Collaboration, automation, and shared responsibility across development and operations |
| Platform Engineering | Providing reusable, self-service capabilities that simplify software delivery |
| Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) | Applying engineering methods to production reliability, scalability, and operations |
| Cloud Engineering | Designing and operating cloud infrastructure and services |

DevOps is largely a set of practices and organizational principles. Platform engineering is one way to operationalize those principles at scale.

SRE focuses on reliability and operational outcomes. A platform team may provide the monitoring, deployment controls, and infrastructure that help SRE and application teams achieve those outcomes.

These are not necessarily separate departments.

A smaller organization may have one team performing all four functions.

### Leadership perspective

The organizational question is not whether the company needs four teams.

It is\:

**Which responsibilities are shared, which are specialized, and how can those capabilities be delivered without creating unnecessary handoffs?**

Creating a dedicated platform team before there is sufficient demand can introduce overhead. Waiting too long can produce extensive duplication and fragmented infrastructure.

## 1.3 The platform engineering value proposition

A successful platform creates value in four dimensions.

**Developer productivity**

Less time configuring infrastructure and more time delivering features

**Security & compliance**

Secure defaults, consistent controls, and auditability

**Operational reliability**

Consistent observability, deployments, and recovery practices

**Organizational scale**

Reusable capabilities that reduce duplicated work across teams

However, platform engineering is not automatically valuable.

If developers must submit tickets to a central team for every deployment, the organization may have centralized complexity rather than removed it.

**Key principle\:** A platform should reduce the cognitive load of application teams without hiding information they need to operate their systems.

---

# Module 2 — Internal Developer Platforms & Architecture

25 minutes

## 2.1 What is an Internal Developer Platform?

An Internal Developer Platform (IDP) is a collection of integrated capabilities that allows developers to build, deploy, operate, and maintain applications with minimal unnecessary infrastructure work.

An IDP is not necessarily one software application.

It is often a combination of\:

- Developer portal or CLI
- Service templates
- CI/CD workflows
- Infrastructure as Code
- Cloud infrastructure
- Identity and access management
- Observability
- Security and compliance controls
- Service ownership and documentation

The developer portal is only the interface to the platform. The platform itself includes the systems and processes that fulfill developer requests.

## 2.2 Reference architecture

A conceptual platform architecture. Security, identity, and governance operate across every layer rather than being confined to a single component.

### The developer experience layer

This is how application teams interact with the platform.

For example, a developer requests a new .NET API service through a portal.

They select\:

- Service name
- Owning team
- Runtime
- Environment requirements
- Database requirements
- Deployment region

The developer should not need to understand every Azure resource or Kubernetes configuration involved.

### The orchestration layer

The platform translates that request into repeatable operations.

It might\:

1. Generate a repository using an approved template.
2. Configure GitHub Actions.
3. Provision infrastructure using Terraform or Bicep.
4. Configure workload identity and secrets.
5. Register the service in a catalog.
6. Establish logging, metrics, and alerts.
7. Deploy an initial application version.

This is the layer where platform engineering turns operational knowledge into automation.

### The infrastructure layer

This contains the actual resources\:

- Azure Kubernetes Service
- Azure Container Apps
- Azure SQL Database
- Azure Service Bus
- Azure Key Vault
- Networking and private endpoints
- Monitoring services

The platform should abstract common complexity while allowing developers to understand and troubleshoot the underlying systems when necessary.

## 2.3 Control plane versus data plane

This distinction becomes important when platforms grow.

**Control plane\:** Manages configuration and desired state.

Examples include provisioning a new service, applying policy, or configuring deployment workflows.

**Data plane\:** Performs the application's actual work, such as serving HTTP requests, processing Kafka messages, or reading from databases.

A developer portal may be part of the platform control plane. The production application running in Kubernetes is part of the workload data plane.

This separation matters because a platform control-plane outage should not automatically take down healthy production applications.

For example, a portal outage may prevent new service provisioning while existing APIs continue serving requests.

Architectural decisions should explicitly consider the failure independence of these layers.

## 2.4 Build versus buy versus integrate

A platform team does not need to build everything.

| Capability | Common approach |
|--------|--------|
| Developer portal | Backstage or a commercial platform |
| Source control | GitHub or GitLab |
| CI/CD | GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps, or another delivery system |
| Infrastructure provisioning | Terraform, OpenTofu, or Bicep |
| Container orchestration | Kubernetes or managed container services |
| Secrets | Azure Key Vault or another managed secrets system |
| Observability | Azure Monitor, Datadog, Grafana, or similar |
| Policy enforcement | Cloud-native policy tools, OPA, or Kyverno |

The architecture should integrate existing tools through stable contracts.

Building a custom developer portal can be justified when workflows are highly specialized. But creating custom replacements for mature infrastructure tools generally introduces significant maintenance obligations.

### Leadership decision

Before approving a custom platform component, determine\:

- What organizational problem cannot be solved by existing tools?
- How many teams need the capability?
- What is the lifetime maintenance cost?
- Who owns upgrades, security patches, documentation, and support?
- What happens if the original engineers leave?

A platform component is not finished when it first works. It becomes an ongoing internal product.

---

# Module 3 — Golden Paths & Developer Experience

20 minutes

## 3.1 What is a golden path?

A golden path is a recommended, supported way to perform a common engineering task.

For example, an organization might provide a golden path for creating .NET microservices.

That path includes\:

- Standard project structure
- Dependency injection configuration
- Health checks
- Structured logging
- Authentication middleware
- Container configuration
- CI/CD workflows
- Observability defaults
- Deployment templates

Instead of spending several days configuring these components, developers start from a known, production-ready foundation.

Golden paths are often called *paved roads*\.

The purpose is to make the recommended approach the easiest practical approach.

## 3.2 Golden paths versus mandatory standards

This is one of the most important platform engineering trade-offs.

| Golden path | Mandatory standard |
|--------|--------|
| Recommended implementation | Required implementation |
| Optimized for convenience | Optimized for consistency or control |
| Alternatives may be supported | Exceptions require approval |
| Encourages adoption | Enforces compliance |
| Appropriate for many implementation choices | Appropriate for critical security or regulatory requirements |

For example, a platform might recommend .NET for internal APIs while allowing Python or Java where justified.

However, every production service may be required to implement authentication, encryption, and minimum observability controls.

**Leadership principle\:** Standardize the outcomes that must be consistent, and preserve flexibility where implementation differences are acceptable.

## 3.3 Cognitive load and developer productivity

A developer's primary responsibility should be delivering business capabilities.

But enterprise development often requires substantial knowledge of infrastructure, deployment, security, and operations.

A platform reduces the amount of knowledge required for routine work.

This does not mean developers should become ignorant of infrastructure.

It means they should not need to repeatedly reconstruct operational details that can be standardized.

Consider a developer implementing a new API.

Without a platform, they might need to understand 15 separate infrastructure concerns before deployment.

With a platform, they might select a service template, provide a small amount of configuration, and deploy through an approved workflow.

The complexity still exists, but it is managed in a reusable system.

### The abstraction danger

Excessive abstraction can become harmful.

If the platform hides all deployment details, developers may struggle to diagnose\:

- Memory exhaustion
- Container startup failures
- Networking problems
- Identity failures
- Resource limits
- Application scaling behavior

A strong platform offers sensible defaults, clear documentation, useful diagnostics, and an escape hatch for legitimate advanced requirements.

## 3.4 Developer portals and service catalogs

A service catalog answers questions such as\:

- What applications exist?
- Who owns each service?
- Where is its repository?
- Where is it deployed?
- What dependencies does it have?
- What is its operational health?
- How can another team consume it?

Tools such as entity["software","Backstage","Open-source developer portal framework"] provide a foundation for service catalogs and developer portals.

A catalog is only valuable if its information stays accurate.

Automated synchronization with source control, deployment systems, and cloud resources is generally more sustainable than manual documentation alone.

### Enterprise example

Suppose an organization has 200 microservices.

During an incident, engineers need to determine which team owns a failing Kafka consumer.

A reliable catalog can provide ownership, runbooks, dashboards, deployment history, and dependencies.

This turns the platform into an operational discovery system, not merely a service-creation tool.

---

# Module 4 — Cloud Infrastructure & Platform Operations

25 minutes

## 4.1 Infrastructure as Code

Infrastructure as Code (IaC) is foundational because platform capabilities must be repeatable.

IaC allows infrastructure to be defined, reviewed, versioned, and provisioned through automated workflows.

Common approaches include\:

- Terraform or OpenTofu for multi-provider infrastructure.
- Bicep for Azure-native resource definitions.
- Pulumi for infrastructure defined through programming languages.

The architectural value is not simply replacing manual clicks with scripts.

It is establishing **reviewable, repeatable infrastructure changes with predictable lifecycle management**\.

A mature platform also manages state, drift detection, permissions, versioning, and recovery from partial provisioning failures.

## 4.2 Kubernetes is not the platform

Kubernetes is a container orchestration system.

It manages workloads, scheduling, scaling, networking integrations, and desired-state reconciliation.

It does not automatically provide a complete developer experience.

An organization can operate Kubernetes successfully while still requiring developers to manually manage YAML files, secrets, deployment workflows, and monitoring.

Conversely, an organization can implement platform engineering without Kubernetes.

For example, a platform built on Azure Container Apps, App Service, GitHub Actions, and Azure Key Vault may satisfy the organization's requirements with less operational overhead.

### Choosing a runtime

| Runtime | Advantages | Trade-offs |
|--------|--------|--------|
| Azure App Service | Simple application hosting and operations | Less control over runtime infrastructure |
| Azure Container Apps | Managed container hosting and scaling | Less control than managing Kubernetes directly |
| Azure Kubernetes Service | Extensive orchestration and extensibility | Greater operational and security complexity |
| Virtual Machines | Maximum OS and runtime control | Greater patching, provisioning, and maintenance burden |

For most organizations, the right runtime is the least complex option that reliably satisfies workload requirements.

Kubernetes should be chosen for capabilities the organization actually needs, not simply because it is widely adopted.

## 4.3 Multi-tenancy and isolation

A shared platform often supports many teams, applications, or customers.

Multi-tenancy introduces architectural questions\:

- Should teams share Kubernetes clusters?
- Should applications share databases?
- How should secrets be isolated?
- How should resource quotas be enforced?
- How can one team's workload affect another?
- How are costs attributed?

There are several isolation models.

Shared infrastructure

Lower infrastructure duplication, but requires stronger tenant isolation, resource controls, and governance.

---

Dedicated infrastructure

Stronger isolation and independent change control, but higher cost and operational duplication.

Shared infrastructure is often attractive for cost efficiency and standardization.

Dedicated infrastructure can be justified for strict compliance boundaries, specialized workloads, performance isolation, or independent release requirements.

Kubernetes namespaces alone should not be assumed to provide a complete security boundary. Strong isolation may require separate clusters, identities, networks, and policy enforcement.

## 4.4 CI/CD as a platform capability

A mature platform provides reusable deployment workflows.

Instead of every team implementing its own pipeline, the platform supplies approved workflows for\:

- Building and testing
- Dependency and vulnerability scanning
- Artifact publishing
- Deployment
- Verification
- Rollback
- Audit reporting

The platform team owns the common workflow implementation.

Application teams own their application-specific build requirements, deployment readiness, and production behavior.

### Important trade-off: centralized versus distributed pipelines

Centralized workflows improve consistency and security.

But they also create shared dependencies.

If a common workflow breaks, many teams may lose the ability to deploy.

This is why shared workflows need versioning, compatibility guarantees, canary adoption, and rollback strategies.

**A platform change affecting 100 services should be managed with the same rigor as a production application change affecting 100 customers.**

---

# Module 5 — Security, Governance & Reliability

20 minutes

## 5.1 Security by default

One of platform engineering's strongest advantages is the ability to make secure behavior automatic.

For example, an approved service template could automatically configure\:

- Workload identity rather than long-lived credentials.
- Secrets retrieval through Azure Key Vault.
- TLS and secure networking defaults.
- Dependency scanning.
- Container image scanning.
- Structured audit logging.
- Least-privilege access.
- Approved deployment environments.

Security becomes part of the standard development workflow rather than a separate process performed near release.

This approach is sometimes described as *shifting security left*\.

However, security is not simply shifted onto developers. The platform should provide reusable controls so teams do not need to become experts in every security implementation.

## 5.2 Policy as Code

Policy as Code allows organizations to express governance rules in machine-enforceable form.

Examples\:

- Production resources must use approved regions.
- Public access to sensitive databases is prohibited.
- Container images must originate from approved registries.
- Deployments must meet security requirements.
- Workloads must declare resource limits.
- Sensitive data must use approved encryption and access controls.

Policies can be enforced at different points.

| Enforcement point | Example |
|--------|--------|
| Pull request | Reject insecure infrastructure definitions |
| CI pipeline | Block an artifact that fails required security checks |
| Deployment admission | Reject a Kubernetes workload violating policy |
| Cloud governance | Deny creation of prohibited cloud resources |
| Runtime monitoring | Detect and report configuration drift |

A well-designed governance system distinguishes between preventive controls, detective controls, and exceptions.

Not every policy needs to block deployment. Some risks can be managed through monitoring and remediation.
